sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax
sections.html:
Property tax in Massachusetts is a town-by-town matter. All 351 cities and towns assess and collect it themselves, which means your bill is set by the municipality and not the county. The Division of Local Services, part of the Department of Revenue, oversees the system, and your local board of assessors holds the property record card for your house.

Value is set as of January 1 for the fiscal year that follows. Fiscal year 2025, for example, runs July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025, and its valuation date is January 1, 2024. That gap explains why a bill can reflect a value set well before you list the house.

Proposition 2½ limits what a city or town can raise in total, not what any single owner pays. There are two restrictions: the levy cannot exceed 2.5% of the community's total assessed value, and the yearly increase is capped at 2.5% of the prior year's levy limit plus new growth.

Voters can go above that only through an override, a debt exclusion or a capital exclusion.

Your own bill can still change, since the whole levy gets split across every taxable parcel. If neighboring values climb faster than yours, you may pay a smaller share even as your value goes up.

How often you pay depends on your town. Quarterly towns usually collect on four dates a year. Towns that bill twice a year give you about 30 days from the mailing date.

Billing styleGeneral due dates
QuarterlyAugust 1, November 1, February 1, May 1
Twice a yearThirty days from the mailing of the bill

Your actual bill spells out the payment deadline and the abatement deadline. Even when a mortgage company pays through escrow, getting the payment in on time remains your job.

sections.h2: How to apply for an abatement
sections.html:
File an abatement application with your local board of assessors on the approved form, on or before the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill. In quarterly municipalities that date is generally February 1, and in twice-a-year municipalities it is generally 30 days after the bill is mailed.

  • Pick up the form at the local assessors' office.
  • An abatement is a reduction in tax, usually granted when you can show fair cash value is lower than the assessed value. It can also be granted for an exemption or an improper classification.
  • Fair cash value means what an informed buyer and seller would agree to in an open sale where neither is pressured.
  • A mailed application is treated as filed on its postmark date, whether it went by the Postal Service or an approved carrier.

The assessors then get three months to respond. They may deny the request, grant all or part of it, or let it sit, and written notice is due within ten days of any action. If they do nothing, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months, not 90 days.

sections.h2: Appealing to the Appellate Tax Board
sections.html:
File with the Appellate Tax Board within three months of the assessors' action, or within three months of the deemed denial if they never acted. When the notice shows two dates, count from the date of action, not the mailing date.

Three requirements are jurisdictional, meaning the board cannot hear the case without them: timely payment of the tax, a timely abatement application on the approved form, and a timely appeal. No exceptions can be made. There is one narrow relief on payment: the board can still hear an appeal if the tax due for the year is $5,000 or less, or if you paid at least the average tax of one of the three prior years.

  • The filing fee depends on assessed value under the board's Schedule of Entry Fees.
  • Most single-family appeals use the informal procedure, which waives most further appeal rights.
  • It usually takes four months to a year to get a hearing, most single-family hearings last one to two hours, and a decision arrives within roughly three months.

sections.h2: What you must prove at the hearing
sections.html:
You carry the burden. A tax assessment is presumed valid, so you must show that the fair cash value of your house is below the assessed value as of the January 1 valuation date. Saying that the tax went up 20% generally does not succeed.

Bring a detailed description of the house and a copy of the assessors' record card. Add sales of similar homes close in type, location, size, timing and condition, adjusted for any differences. You may also use comparable assessments or hire an expert appraiser. Documents must reach the board and the other side at least seven days before the hearing.

There is one exception to the presumption. If the board set a value for one year and assessors raise it in either of the next two fiscal years, the burden shifts to the assessors to justify the increase.

Skipped property tax, or unpaid water and sewer charges, turns into a lien, and the municipality can end up taking the house. Once a bill is 30 days late it can send a demand. Ignore that demand for 14 days and it can record a tax taking at the Registry of Deeds.

  • After a waiting period of six or twelve months, whoever holds the tax title may start a foreclosure case in the Land Court.
  • A private party can become the tax title owner, for example by buying bundled tax bills or winning an auction.
  • You may answer the complaint and request a hearing. There you can offer to pay off the full balance or propose installments.
  • Miss the payoff date the judge sets and a foreclosure judgment can follow, which cuts off any chance of getting the property back.

If the house was worth more than the debt, a foreclosed owner may be able to claim the difference. It is far easier to settle a tax taking early, before the Land Court gets involved.

Once a tax taking is recorded, it clouds the title and has to be cleared before the sale can close cleanly. Paying everything owed ends the town's claim if you do it before a final foreclosure judgment. Your closing attorney can explain how unpaid tax gets handled at closing.

Ask the collector's office for a payoff figure before you list. Look over the assessors' record for mistakes, and note any abatement deadline that could fall after you sell. What happens to a pending abatement once the house changes hands is something to ask the assessors and your attorney. A cash buyer can often close with the payoff built into the settlement, though the lien still has to be cleared that day.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to file a Massachusetts property tax abatement?
faqs.a: The cutoff is the first installment due date printed on your real tax bill. Quarterly towns usually land on February 1, and twice-a-year towns run about 30 days from mailing. Your bill states the exact date.

faqs.q: How long do assessors have to decide an abatement?
faqs.a: Three months. Silence for three calendar months counts as a denial, and that starts a three-month window to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay the tax while I appeal?
faqs.a: Generally yes. The Appellate Tax Board needs the tax paid on time to have jurisdiction, with limited exceptions when the tax is $5,000 or less or you paid the average of a prior year.
It limits the total levy a municipality can raise. The levy cannot exceed 2.5% of total assessed value, and it can rise by 2.5% of the prior levy limit plus new growth unless voters approve more.

faqs.q: Can the city take my house for unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, in the end. A demand, then 14 days, then a recorded tax taking, and a Land Court foreclosure can follow. Paying all taxes, interest and fees before final judgment lets you redeem.
